threats.name: Capability token theft

mitigations.control: Capabilities are signed, time-bounded, and revocable.
Chio-native DPoP can be required per grant, and hosted sender-constrained sessions can bind to DPoP or mTLS continuity.
High-value clustered deployments should use durable replay state rather than process-local proof nonces alone.

threats.residualRisk: Compatibility profiles still allow bearer-style capability use when sender constraint is not required, and replay protection weakens across restart or failover when nonce state is only process-local.

threats.name: Kernel impersonation

mitigations.control: Capabilities and receipts are signed artifacts and hosted/native version contracts are explicit.
Cross-host deployments are required to use authenticated transport before authority is trusted.
Operators should distribute and pin Chio verifier keys, service certificates, or equivalent trust anchors with stricter rotation discipline.

threats.residualRisk: Plaintext local-development modes intentionally do not provide peer authenticity, and receipt trust still depends on deployment-specific trust-anchor distribution.

threats.name: Tool server escape

mitigations.control: The kernel mediates capability scope, server id, and tool name before invocation.
Production tool-server transport is modeled as an authenticated channel instead of anonymous raw TCP.
Operators should pair Chio mediation with OS or container sandboxing, least-privilege filesystem access, and outbound-network restrictions.

threats.residualRisk: Chio mediation does not by itself sandbox arbitrary tool-server code; a compromised tool process can still abuse whatever host privileges the operator granted it.

threats.name: Replay attacks on the native channel

mitigations.control: Chio-native DPoP can bind a request to capability id, tool target, action hash, freshness, sender key, and nonce uniqueness.
Capabilities are time-bounded and can be revoked.
Replay-sensitive deployments should require DPoP and avoid process-local-only nonce registries for high-value flows.

threats.residualRisk: The native framed lane has no separate in-band anti-replay mechanism outside the sender-proof and capability systems, so non-DPoP grants remain replayable within their validity window if the transport is exposed.

threats.name: Resource exhaustion denial of service

mitigations.control: Native frames larger than 16 MiB are rejected, and hosted sessions keep explicit lifecycle and stream-attachment limits.
Deployments should enforce request-rate, concurrency, and time-budget controls at hosted and trust-control edges.
Operators should bound retained replay buffers, queues, and per-session state and pair Chio with upstream load shedding.

threats.residualRisk: Size checks and lifecycle rules reduce but do not eliminate asymmetric workload attacks, and authenticated callers can still consume their own allowed quota share.

threats.name: Delegation chain abuse

mitigations.control: Trust-control delegated issuance already enforces a signed delegation-policy ceiling when one is supplied.
Chio core exposes delegation-chain and attenuation validators and the runtime already carries revocation state.
High-trust delegated flows should resolve and validate complete parent lineage recursively at admission time rather than trust presented metadata alone.

threats.residualRisk: The shipped runtime is stronger than unchecked delegation metadata, but it is not yet a universally recursive, fail-closed delegated-authority proof system at every entry point.

threats.name: SSRF via HTTP substrate

mitigations.control: The InternalNetworkGuard blocks egress to private, reserved, loopback, link-local, cloud metadata, and Kubernetes addresses.
DNS rebinding detection, encoded IP detection, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 handling catch common obfuscated internal targets.
Deployments exposing HTTP substrate endpoints must enable the InternalNetworkGuard, add deployment-specific internal hostnames, and fail closed on address parse ambiguity.

threats.residualRisk: DNS time-of-check/time-of-use gaps and tool-execution redirects can still reach targets that were not visible in the guarded arguments.

threats.name: PII or PHI exposure in responses

mitigations.control: The ResponseSanitizationGuard scans responses for PII and PHI patterns with configurable sensitivity levels and block or redact actions.
Pre-invocation scanning prevents PII in request arguments from reaching tool servers, and custom patterns support deployment-specific sensitive data.
Healthcare and financial deployments must enable ResponseSanitizationGuard at Medium sensitivity or higher and define custom patterns for local identifiers.

threats.residualRisk: Regex-based pattern detection is incomplete, may false-positive in non-medical contexts, and does not scan image or binary response content.

threats.name: Agent velocity abuse

mitigations.control: The AgentVelocityGuard enforces per-agent and per-session rate limits using token-bucket semantics with configurable burst factors.
Separate buckets per agent and per session isolate one caller's exhaustion from other agents and prevent cross-session token sharing.
Multi-tenant deployments must configure per-agent limits, set per-session limits, and keep burst factors close to 1.0 for high-value operations.

threats.residualRisk: Rate limits are process-local, and an attacker controlling multiple agent identities can multiply the effective allowed rate.

threats.name: Cumulative data exfiltration

mitigations.control: The DataFlowGuard reads cumulative bytes-read and bytes-written totals from the session journal and denies requests when configured limits are exceeded.
The DataTransferAdvisoryGuard provides early warning before hard limits, and the session journal uses saturating arithmetic for data-flow accounting.
Sensitive-data deployments must configure DataFlowGuard limits, promotion rules, and max_bytes_total limits appropriate to their data classification.

threats.residualRisk: Per-session accounting can be bypassed through many short sessions, and byte counts do not measure semantic information density or compression.

threats.name: Behavioral sequence attack

mitigations.control: The BehavioralSequenceGuard enforces required predecessors, forbidden transitions, max consecutive invocations, and required first-tool constraints.
The session journal tracks the complete tool invocation sequence, including denied invocations.
Operators should define forbidden transitions, required initialization tools, and max consecutive limits for deployment-specific dangerous sequences.

threats.residualRisk: The guard cannot prevent cross-session dangerous sequences, non-adjacent forbidden transitions, or semantically dangerous invocations hidden behind benign tool names.

threats.name: WASM guard resource exhaustion

mitigations.control: WASM guards execute under a fuel budget that limits CPU per invocation and fails closed on fuel exhaustion.
WASM guards execute in isolated linear memory with no host filesystem, network, kernel-state, or host-callback access.
Operators must set appropriate fuel limits, test custom guards in advisory mode, and monitor fuel consumption before enabling blocking production guards.

threats.residualRisk: Linear memory pressure within the runtime limit and compilation CPU for pathologically complex modules are not fully capped by Chio fuel metering.

threats.name: Post-quantum signature downgrade

mitigations.control: Signed artifacts that opt into the post-quantum profile will carry policy-visible algorithm metadata so verifiers can reject classical-only substitutions.
Receipt, capability, and compliance-certificate verification will enforce the configured cryptographic floor before accepting an artifact.
Migration tests will cover classical compatibility and post-quantum-required rejection of downgraded signatures.

threats.residualRisk: Until hybrid signature verification and cryptographic-floor enforcement ship, operators must treat post-quantum protection as planned rather than available.

threats.name: TEE quote forgery or misbinding

mitigations.control: Quote verifiers will validate platform evidence for Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and AWS Nitro before accepting a claimed confidential-runtime binding.
Accepted quotes will bind report data to the kernel signing key and receipt root so copied or stale quotes cannot authorize another runtime.
Pinned positive and negative quote fixtures will exercise malformed, stale, and mismatched quote paths.

threats.residualRisk: Until platform quote verification lands, TEE deployment claims depend on external operator evidence and are not independently verified by Chio.
